idiom_name: single state struct + intent enum + pure reduce() + render(state)
implementation_notes: C has no closures, sum types or runtime, so the whole loop is hand-written: the screen state is a struct, intents are a tagged struct (an enum kind plus payload), the reducer is a pure function returning the next state by value, and the view is a function that redraws from a const pointer to the state. Widget callbacks (GTK/GLib signals or a custom event loop) produce intents, and because the language cannot enforce immutability the discipline is convention: the reducer copies the incoming state, the store publishes const snapshots and one function performs every transition. The classic structure is justified for embedded or desktop UIs whose transition table must be replayed and tested off-target; a single-widget tool is simpler with ad-hoc state and a redraw call.
pitfalls: Handing the view a pointer into the live state lets any callback mutate history in place; publish const pointers to copies and replace the state wholesale.
Reading a union or struct member the intent tag did not select is undefined behaviour; switch on the tag before touching the payload.
A global state shared by several screens or threads needs an explicit owner and a queue: dispatching reentrantly from a signal handler or ISR interleaves transitions.
State members that are pointers alias caller buffers; define ownership explicitly or copy the payload into the state.
